Gecko's sandboxes, explained

Every web page in Firefox runs inside a compartment. Code from one compartment can only touch another through wrappers, and the most interesting of them are Xrays.

An Xray lets privileged code look at a page's DOM without seeing anything the page changed in JavaScript: no redefined methods, no getters planted on prototypes. The browser sees the document as the HTML built it.

That is why a content script can call document.querySelector on a hostile page and get the real answer. Only code that waives the Xray on purpose sees the page's own objects, and it then has to treat everything it reads as untrusted.

Sandboxes take the idea one step further. A sandbox is a compartment with a principal of its choosing, which lets an add-on or the browser run code with exactly the rights of a page, or fewer, while it still sees through Xrays to the DOM underneath.

Put together, compartments, wrappers and sandboxes are what let the browser run code from many sources in one process without any of them reaching the others by accident.
